analysis.investment_thesis: Brigade is a Bengaluru-centric real estate developer with improving momentum post-2022, but the business model is inherently cyclical, capital-intensive, and debt-laden — everything I avoid. Negative net profits in FY21 and FY22 prove the earnings fragility that cyclical developers always carry.
key_strengths: Revenue and EBITDA on clear uptrend since FY22 with 10.7% revenue CAGR and 11.8% EBITDA CAGR over 9 years
Leasing and hospitality segments provide some recurring income stability alongside lumpy development revenues
Equity base expanded sharply in FY25 (equity 6,481 Cr vs 3,516 Cr in FY24), suggesting equity raise that has reduced D/E burden somewhat
key_risks: Debt/Equity at 0.76 — more than double my hard limit of 0.3; borrowings at 5,375 Cr with finance costs at 495 Cr eating deeply into profits
Net profits turned negative in FY21 (-96 Cr) and FY22 (-65 Cr) — a clean earnings track record is non-negotiable for me
Promoter holding at only 41.11% is well below my 55% floor, signalling limited skin in the game
red_flags: Debt/Equity 0.76 — hard fail on balance sheet quality
Consecutive years of net losses (FY21, FY22) reveal cyclical vulnerability
Free cash flow collapsed to just 66 Cr in FY24 despite 4,897 Cr revenue — capital efficiency is poor
Finance costs (495 Cr in FY25) represent 73% of net profit — dangerously leveraged earnings
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Brigade operates in a sector I fundamentally distrust for long-term equity compounding — real estate development requires massive upfront capital, is hostage to regulatory approvals, interest rate cycles, and unsold inventory, and produces lumpy, unpredictable earnings. The data confirms this: revenues swung from 2,973 Cr in FY19 to 1,950 Cr in FY21, and the company reported net losses two years running. The recent recovery is real (FY25 PAT 680 Cr, 19.3% PAT CAGR), but it follows a deep trough and is partly flattered by other income of 233 Cr.

The balance sheet is the decisive dealbreaker for me. Borrowings of 5,375 Cr against equity of 6,481 Cr gives D/E of 0.83 on borrowings alone (0.76 reported), and finance costs at 495 Cr annually represent nearly 9% of total debt — a heavy carry. ROE of 14.9% is below my 15% threshold and ROCE of 13.3% is disappointing for the risk. With promoters at 41% and real estate being inherently disruption-prone from online listings, REITs, and co-working, I would not deploy capital here.
